Front Door Premium
Understand. Deploy. Operate.

A practical guide to this repository: protect your existing Web Apps, deploy with one configuration file, and manage future changes with Terraform.

Scope Premium · Private Link · WAF
Workflow Standard Terraform
State Local first
Updated 23 October 2026
READ FIRST

One file to configure. Standard Terraform to deploy.

This guide explains the repository as delivered: what it creates, how it connects to your existing application, and how your team operates it. It is a reusable customer handover, so names and regional choices remain your inputs.

First deployment: the repository README is the main checklist. This self-contained guide is an alternative reading format; you do not need to complete both. Review the starting settings below, then follow the deployment steps. For ongoing work, use the change recipes. WAF behavior is explained separately. Deployment uses standard Terraform; no Python tooling is included.
You configure

terraform.tfvars
Names, existing apps, routes, regions and WAF options.

Terraform deploys

Front Door Premium, WAF and the child resources described below.

You verify

Approve the private connection, test the real application and confirm a no-change plan.

Status: the baseline is implemented. Isolated Azure testing with Terraform 1.17.0 verified private application routing, WAF behavior, failover and shared-state migration. Customer deployment and application acceptance still remain; see the tested scope.

Starting configuration at a glance

SettingSingle-app starter
Front DoorPremium, global, one public endpoint.
Resource group and Private LinkWest Europe (westeurope) in the example. Keep both for an app in West Europe; neither relocates the app.
Application routingOne existing Web App, all paths (/*), HTTPS forwarding, caching off.
Health probeHTTPS GET /health; replace the path with one the app actually serves.
WAFDetection: inspection without blocking. Review external logs, tune, then select Prevention.
StateLocal initially; migrate before teammates deploy.
01 · ARCHITECTURE

How a request reaches your application

  1. The client connects to the Front Door public endpoint over HTTPS.
  2. The WAF evaluates the request under the policy attached to that endpoint. A blocking decision ends the request at the edge.
  3. The matching route selects an origin group. Initially /* routes to the first Web App.
  4. Front Door forwards to the origin over HTTPS using its managed Private Link connection.
  5. The existing application serves the request. Its public network access is disabled by its owner, closing the direct public bypass.

Front Door creates its private endpoint in a Microsoft-managed regional network. Front Door and the Web App do not need to share a customer VNet. This repository does not need to deploy a customer VNet or private DNS zone for that connection. The app owner must approve it before private traffic works. Public access and the private connection can coexist during migration. Explicitly set public access to Enabled in the app’s authoritative configuration if it must remain public during staging; an unset value can default to Disabled once a private endpoint exists. Keep existing access restrictions. Direct public requests allowed by the app bypass Front Door and its WAF. Disable public access after verifying the private path and completing cutover.

02 · OWNERSHIP

What is deployed—and who manages each part

The single-app example produces the baseline below. Maps allow more instances later. A profile identity is a property of the profile; it is not a new application deployment.

ComponentBaseline behaviorOwner
Resource groupCreates a dedicated group when resource_group.create=true; otherwise reads an existing group.Terraform / platform team
Front Door Premium profileCreates the profile with a system-assigned identity.Terraform
EndpointCreates the public endpoint and returns its generated hostname.Terraform
Origin group + originCreates the routing configuration pointing to the existing app, with HTTPS probes and required Private Link settings.Terraform
RouteCreates /*, redirects HTTP to HTTPS and forwards HTTPS to the origin. Caching is off by default.Terraform
WAF policy + associationCreates the enabled policy and associates it with the endpoint on /*. Defaults are explained below.Terraform
Private connection requestFront Door creates its managed connection request from the origin configuration.Azure creates it; app owner approves
Existing Web App and App Service planReferenced by ID/hostname. App code, scaling, authentication and public-access settings remain in the app stack.Application team
Diagnostics and Event HubNo diagnostic settings, Event Hubs or Log Analytics resources are created here.Separate diagnostics application
DNS and custom certificatesNot required for the first generated-hostname deployment. Optional domain/certificate references are supported.DNS/certificate owner with Terraform configuration
State storageLocal initially. Shared storage has a separate lifecycle and is adopted later.Deployment operator / platform team
Optional only: custom domains, certificate references, scoped identity role assignments, rule sets, additional endpoints/origins/routes and extra WAF policies are created only when their inputs are supplied. No test application, HTTP Echo container, database, Kubernetes cluster or logging destination is part of this repository.

Why this design: Premium satisfies the requested Private Link connectivity. Explicit maps and names support customer conventions and future expansion. Existing apps keep their own ownership, and separate diagnostics ownership avoids competing configuration of the same diagnostic settings.

04 · BEFORE DEPLOYMENT

Collect the customer values once

Install Terraform 1.17.0 and Azure CLI. The root constraint is ~> 5.10.0; the checked-in lock selects AzureRM 5.10.0. Example names below are placeholders, not a required customer convention.

InputWhere it goesHow to choose
Subscription UUIDsubscription_idSubscription that will contain Front Door.
Resource groupresource_groupCustomer name, metadata location and create=true/false.
Profile and endpoint namesfront_door.name; endpoints.public.nameCustomer naming convention; endpoint name must be available.
Existing app ID/hostnameorigin_groups.web.origins.primaryCopy the full production app resource ID and actual default hostname from Azure.
Private Link locationOrigin’s private_link.locationSupported Front Door regional location near the app; confirm residency requirements.
Probe pathGroup’s health_probe.pathExisting lightweight path returning HTTP 200 without interactive login.

Understand the region choices

The starter explicitly sets both location inputs to westeurope. These are example values, not module fallbacks. Keep them for an existing app in West Europe.

SettingEffect
Front Door edgeGlobal; no region selector for placing the endpoint in one app region.
resource_group.locationMetadata location when creating a group; changing it forces replacement. Ignored when reusing an existing group.
private_link.locationRegional managed private connection for an origin. Changing it replaces the Front Door origin and requires approval of the new connection.
Existing app locationOwned by the app stack. Changing these Terraform settings does not move the app or its data.

Access and application readiness

  • The deployment identity needs resource-management rights in the target group and group-creation rights if creating one. Optional role assignments need additional role-assignment permission at their scope.
  • The subscription administrator registers Microsoft.Cdn and Microsoft.Network. The existing app subscription uses Microsoft.Web. This provider configuration disables automatic provider registration.
  • The app owner confirms its plan supports Private Endpoints, HTTPS-only is enabled, the health path works, and a production site rather than a deployment slot is used.
  • The app owner must explicitly disable public network access for the private baseline and retain an appropriate deployment/SCM access path.

05 · FIRST DEPLOYMENT

Follow these five steps in order

Run the commands from the repository root. These examples use a Bash/zsh terminal; the file copy can also be done in your editor. No Python command is required.

1. Sign in

az login

Use the account/tenant authorized for the selected subscription. The provider receives the target subscription from terraform.tfvars.

2. Copy and fill the configuration

cp examples/single-app/terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars

Replace the zero UUID, names, app hostname/resource ID, health path and tags. Keep the West Europe location values when appropriate for the existing app. Preserve map keys such as public, web and primary after deployment; those keys identify Terraform instances. Use either terraform.tfvars or terraform.tfvars.json, not both.

View the complete single-app example
# Copy to terraform.tfvars at the repository root and replace every placeholder.
# Start: README.md. All inputs/defaults: docs/reference.md.
# Keep one checkout/state per environment; do not switch environments in the same local state.
# 1. Customer subscription, resource group and tags.
subscription_id = "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"
resource_group = {
  name     = "rg-customer-edge-dev"
  location = "westeurope" # Resource-group metadata only. Front Door is GLOBAL.
  create   = true
}
tags = {
  customer    = "customer"
  environment = "dev"
  owner       = "platform-team"
}

# 2. Customer names. Keep keys such as public/web/primary stable after deployment.
front_door = {
  name = "afd-customer-dev"
  endpoints = {
    public = { name = "fde-customer-dev-unique" }
  }
  # 3. Existing app and its private connection. This does not create an app.
  origin_groups = {
    web = {
      name = "og-web"
      # Replace /health with an existing unauthenticated path that returns HTTP 200.
      health_probe = { path = "/health", request_type = "GET" }
      origins = {
        primary = {
          name = "origin-web-primary"
          # Use defaultHostName returned by Azure; newer apps can have regional hostnames.
          host_name = "replace-with-existing-app.azurewebsites.net"
          private_link = {
            target_resource_id = "/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/rg-existing-app/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/replace-with-existing-app"
            target_type        = "sites"
            location           = "westeurope" # Supported Front Door Private Link region near THIS app.
            request_message    = "afd-customer-dev: web primary"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
  # 4. URL routing. The first app receives all paths.
  routes = {
    web = {
      name              = "route-web"
      endpoint_key      = "public"
      origin_group_key  = "web"
      patterns_to_match = ["/*"]
    }
  }
}

# 5. Customer WAF names. Inspection starts in Detection (no blocking).
waf_policies = {
  default = {
    name                 = "wafcustomerdev"
    security_policy_name = "security-default"
    # Defaults: Detection, body inspection, DRS 2.1 and Bot Manager 1.1.
    # Enable external WAF logs, tune, then set mode = "Prevention".
  }
}
Optional: read app details with Azure CLI
az webapp show --subscription '<app-subscription-id>' \
  --resource-group '<existing-app-resource-group>' --name '<existing-app-name>' \
  --query '{id:id,host:defaultHostName,location:location}'

3. Initialize, review and deploy

terraform init -lockfile=readonly
terraform apply

terraform apply displays the plan and waits for confirmation. Review the names, app targets and changes, then type yes only when correct. The single-app example creates eight resources with a new resource group, or seven in an existing group. Expected: apply completes and reports outputs. The private connection may still need approval; provisioning is not a traffic-readiness test.

4. Approve the private connection in Azure

  1. The app owner opens the existing App Service → Networking → Configure your private endpoint connections.
  2. Inspect the pending request for this deployment. Check the intended app, request details and creation time; the description alone is not proof of its source.
  3. Approve that specific request and confirm it becomes Approved. Do not approve unrelated requests.

Allow the connection and edge configuration to propagate before declaring success.

5. Verify the real application

terraform output endpoint_urls

Copy the public HTTPS URL from the output. Azure generates its hostname; do not guess it from the endpoint resource name. For all IDs and configuration details, use terraform output -json front_door.

CheckExpected result
Open https://<hostname>/<health-path>The expected app response, not merely an arbitrary HTTP 200.
Test the real pages/API/login flowsNormal customer behavior works; legitimate requests are not unexpectedly blocked.
Open the same URL with HTTPRedirects to HTTPS.
Use the app’s direct default hostname from a public networkPublic access denied; confirm Public network access is Disabled in Azure. Existing private network clients may still reach it privately.
Check WAF policy and association in AzureThe chosen mode is active and the intended endpoint/domain is covered.
Run terraform plan againNo changes. A nonempty plan needs review.
Finished means: infrastructure exists, the private connection is approved, the application checks pass, the agreed WAF mode is active, and the follow-up plan is empty. Keep state/configuration protected and assign an operator. A Detection trial is not equivalent to enforcing WAF blocks.
Verified sourcesApproval procedure

If this app already serves public production traffic

Use a staged cutover: if public users must retain access, explicitly set publicNetworkAccess=Enabled in the app’s authoritative configuration first and preserve its access restrictions; deploy the edge; approve and test the private path; complete customer DNS/certificate onboarding if needed; move traffic when ready; then have the app owner disable public access and verify no public bypass remains. Account for DNS TTLs and deployment-agent access. Changing publicNetworkAccess restarts Linux Web Apps, so schedule that change in the cutover window. Do not disable an active public application without that cutover plan.

06 · WAF EXPLAINED

“All paths” does not mean “block everything”

WAF coverage and WAF mode answer two different questions: where do we inspect? and what do we do with a matching request?

SettingMeaningThis repository
Coverage /*Inspect requests across all URL paths on the associated endpoint/domain, including /, /login and /api/orders.Enforced by the security association; routes are not silently left outside WAF coverage.
Prevention modeEnforce configured actions, including blocking decisions. Normal requests continue unless another configured action applies.Select explicitly after tuning to enforce WAF rules.
Detection modeEvaluate matches without enforcing blocking actions.Default for onboarding; no blocking. Configure external WAF log delivery before tuning.

It is enabled because this deployment introduces a public entry point. Private Link protects the connection to the app; WAF evaluates the public web request. WAF is not the application’s login or authorization system, and it does not decide access merely from the fact that a URL exists.

What rules are active initially?

The repository defaults to Microsoft Default Rule Set 2.1 and Bot Manager 1.1, with rule-set action Block, plus request-body inspection. The single-app example defines no custom rules. With DRS 2.1, matching rules contribute to anomaly scoring; an individual match does not always cause an immediate block. At the blocking threshold, the configured action and policy mode determine the outcome. Bot and custom rules can have their own actions.

Example: a normal GET /products that triggers no blocking decision proceeds. A request that reaches a managed blocking decision or matches a configured custom Block rule is stopped in Prevention. A legitimate request can also match a rule, which is why application testing and narrow tuning matter.

How the customer selects the mode

# Inside the existing waf_policies.default object in terraform.tfvars:
mode = "Detection"
# After reviewing external WAF logs and tuning, change to "Prevention".
# Keep the existing name, security_policy_name and any rule settings.

Make this edit inside the existing policy object, then generate and review a new plan and apply it. Detection is the repository default. Existing deployments that omit mode will inherit it on upgrade: explicitly retain mode = "Prevention" if already enforcing.

A practical tuning sequence

  1. Test the real application flows in a non-production environment. Start with the default Detection mode for an agreed tuning window.
  2. Have the separate diagnostics application enable the relevant WAF log export to Event Hub and confirm the consumer can read it. This repository does not enable that export.
  3. Identify the exact rule and request field behind a false positive. Add a narrowly scoped exclusion or override; avoid broad Allow rules that bypass later evaluation.
  4. Switch to Prevention, retest normal behavior and a controlled blocking case, and monitor through the external diagnostics system.

07 · CHANGE MANAGEMENT

Manage the deployment through the same file

Edit terraform.tfvars, run terraform apply, review its displayed plan and confirm the intended changes. Then verify the affected application paths.

terraform apply
# Review the displayed plan, then type yes.
# Approve any new private connection, then test application traffic.
terraform plan
ChangeEditVerify
Add an independent app/APIAdd an origin group with its origin, then a route referring to that group.Approve its connection; test new and existing paths.
Add a replica of the same appAdd another origin in the existing group.Compatible app/data/auth behavior; test health and failover.
Change pathsEdit route patterns_to_match.Include both /api and /api/* when needed.
Strip the API route prefixSet origin_path = "/" on the API route.Confirm /api/orders reaches the app as /orders.
Change WAF behaviorEdit the selected policy’s mode, custom rules, exclusions or managed overrides.Normal app flows plus the intended blocking case.
Change probesEdit the origin group’s health probe.HTTP 200 with the configured GET/HEAD method.
Change a Private Link regionPrefer adding a new origin/connection, validating it, then retiring the old one.Editing the existing location replaces the origin; dependent routes update and a new approval is required. Changing RG location does not move the app.
Enable cachingAdd cache to the intended static route.Cache key and headers; do not casually cache personalized/authenticated responses.
Remove an originRemove or redirect dependent routes first, then retire the origin/group.No route depends on it; the app itself remains in its app stack.

Example: add an existing API alongside the first app

Insert these two entries into the existing maps. Do not paste a second front_door variable or duplicate the existing map definitions.

# Add this entry inside front_door.origin_groups:
api = {
  name = "og-api"
  health_probe = { path = "/health", request_type = "GET" }
  origins = {
    primary = {
      name      = "origin-api-primary"
      host_name = "replace-with-existing-api.azurewebsites.net"
      private_link = {
        target_resource_id = "/subscriptions/<app-subscription>/resourceGroups/<app-rg>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<api-app>"
        target_type        = "sites"
        location           = "<supported-private-link-region>"
        request_message    = "customer-profile: api primary"
      }
    }
  }
}

# Add this entry inside front_door.routes:
api = {
  name              = "route-api"
  endpoint_key      = "public"
  origin_group_key  = "api"
  patterns_to_match = ["/api", "/api/*"]
}

The catch-all web route can remain. More-specific API patterns select the API route; the forwarded path remains /api/… unless you configure an origin path or rewrite. On this API route, origin_path = "/" removes the matched API prefix. The API probe still uses its configured /health path. See docs/configuration.md for the supported rewrite, header and WAF examples.

When rule execution order matters, keep those rules in one rule set and use unique order values. AzureRM stores route rule-set associations as a set; the position of keys in rule_set_keys does not guarantee execution order.

Replicas and regions

For active/passive replicas, use priority 1 for primary and 2 for standby. For weighted sharing, use the same priority and configure weights. Health and latency participate in selection, so weights are not guaranteed exact percentages. A new regional app and data replication must already be prepared by the app team. Test a standby through a controlled failure or a temporary independent test route before relying on it.

Stable keys matter: renaming web or primary can change Terraform resource addresses. Renaming Azure resources can also force replacement. Review every replacement; use deliberate state refactoring for key-only changes.

08 · OPTIONAL EXPANSION

Domains, identities and diagnostics

Customer DNS and HTTPS certificates

Begin with the generated endpoint hostname. When the customer needs a branded hostname, add a custom domain in front_door.custom_domains, publish the required DNS ownership record using custom_domain_validation, wait for validation/certificate readiness, and associate the domain with its route. The DNS owner points the hostname to the actual output endpoint hostname when ready. DNS records are not created by this repository.

The module defaults to an Azure-managed certificate for a custom domain. Customer-managed certificates can instead reference an existing Key Vault certificate. Stage domain validation before serving production traffic; a pending certificate is not a completed onboarding.

To remove a customer domain, first detach it from every route and apply while retaining the domain object. Then remove the domain and apply. If a route loses its last domain, remove that route or deliberately choose its replacement hostname; do not accidentally expose the default hostname.

Managed identity has a specific job here

The Front Door profile always receives a system-assigned identity. The configuration can attach existing user-assigned identities and create scoped role assignments for the system-assigned identity, for example for supported Key Vault certificate access. The app’s own identity and downstream data access remain in its application stack.

Private Link limitation: Front Door managed-identity bearer-token authentication to origins is not supported for Private Link origins. This implementation does not claim to authenticate private Web App requests using the profile identity. Application authentication must still be designed by the app team.

Logging is externally owned

Pass front_door.profile_id to the separate diagnostics application. That application creates/manages diagnostic settings and Event Hub delivery. This Terraform stack contains no diagnostic-setting resources, Log Analytics workspace or Event Hub destination. Organizational Azure Policy may independently add a setting. Coordinate its ownership with the platform team; each setting needs a distinct name and one owner. Agree which team monitors availability, origin health and WAF events, and confirm that exported logs arrive.

09 · LATER, BEFORE TEAM OPERATION

Move local state to shared Azure Blob storage

This is not required for the first single-operator deployment. Local state records resource ownership on that machine; it is unrelated to serving web traffic. Before teammates operate the same deployment, migrate the authoritative state and give them the same code, lock file and environment configuration.

  1. The platform team provides a separate storage account/container, appropriate network access and Entra ID data-plane permissions. Prefer the scoped Storage Blob Data Contributor role for authorized state operators, with versioning/soft-delete and protected backups.
  2. Pause all applies. Back up the authoritative state outside the repository in an existing protected location.
terraform state pull > /secure/backup/frontdoor-before-migration.tfstate
terraform state list > /secure/backup/frontdoor-addresses.txt

Replace /secure/backup with your protected directory. State may contain sensitive data.

  1. Copy the inactive backend examples and fill the storage coordinates. Choose a unique key per customer/environment and an unused destination.
cp backend.tf.example backend.tf
cp examples/remote.backend.hcl.example customer.backend.hcl
Backend configuration example
# Nonsecret backend coordinates. Never put access keys, SAS tokens or client secrets here.
storage_account_name = "stcustomerterraform"
container_name       = "tfstate"
key                  = "customer/dev/frontdoor.tfstate"
use_azuread_auth     = true
use_cli              = true
  1. From the existing directory that owns the state, migrate it. Review Terraform’s source/destination prompt.
terraform init -migrate-state -backend-config=customer.backend.hcl
  1. Confirm the remote blob exists, resource IDs/lineage match the backup, and terraform plan proposes no recreation. Keep recovery backups protected.
  2. A teammate obtains the same reviewed code, backend block/coordinates and terraform.tfvars, then initializes the already-migrated backend:
terraform init -backend-config=customer.backend.hcl
terraform plan

Blob locking coordinates state access; still serialize applies. Sharing state does not synchronize variable files. Do not use -reconfigure instead of -migrate-state for the initial move, and do not run an apply against an accidentally empty backend. The full recovery/networking checklist is in docs/remote-state.md.

10 · OPERATIONS

Maintain, troubleshoot and recover

WhenAction
After every changeTest affected routes and normal user flows; confirm a no-change plan.
During normal operationUse the separately owned monitoring/diagnostics system. A Terraform plan does not test availability.
At configuration reviewRun a plan to detect drift. Investigate unexpected changes before applying; review WAF false positives narrowly.
Before an upgradeRead release notes, change constraints deliberately, run terraform init -upgrade in non-production, review the lock/plan and test before production.
Before removing a resourceReview dependencies and DNS/diagnostics ownership; keep state until deletion completes.
SymptomCheck first
403 through Front DoorWAF decision versus application authorization. Use the external WAF logs and request reference; do not assume every 403 is WAF.
502/503Expected private connection approved, app healthy, correct target/hostname/host header and certificate.
404 or wrong appActual output hostname, enabled route, matching domain/path, app path expectations and propagation.
Direct public app still worksApp public-network access was not explicitly disabled, or the test machine is using a separate private path.
Domain fails but default endpoint worksDNS ownership, certificate readiness, route/domain association and DNS target.
Plan proposes many replacementsWrong state/environment, changed stable keys or changed immutable resource names. Stop and investigate.

Rollback: restore the previous desired configuration, generate a fresh plan and apply it after review. Reusing an old saved plan is not a rollback procedure. After an interrupted apply, preserve state and re-plan; do not delete state to forget the error.

Retirement: coordinate traffic, DNS and external diagnostics, review terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan, then deliberately apply that plan. Existing apps are not managed by this stack. A resource group created by this stack must not contain unrelated resources that would be lost when it is deleted.

11 · VALIDATION

What has actually been tested

Live Azure validation completed with Terraform 1.17.0 and AzureRM 5.10.0 on 23 October 2026 (Israel time). The tests used the customer root configuration with disposable existing-app fixtures. No customer application was modified.

Verified areaEvidence
Native checksFormatting, validation and 16 native Terraform test runs passed, including both customer examples, Detection defaults, explicit Prevention and existing-group/usable-URL checks. Eight configuration-guide snippets also passed separate mock plans.
Provisioning and updatesThe first example created 8 resources; the existing-resource-group variant created 7. The expanded deployment managed 31 resources and converged to a no-change plan.
Real HTTP behavior32 checks passed: private web/API routing, origin paths and rewrites, redirects, headers, caching/compression, affinity, WAF modes/actions/exclusions and rate limiting.
Failover and recoveryStopping the test primary selected the backup after about 81 seconds. Restarting restored primary responses after about 82 seconds. These observations are not an availability guarantee.
Identity and security settingsAzure API checks verified the system/user identities, scoped Key Vault role, HTTPS settings, disabled resources and all-path WAF associations. The latest run verified that Terraform owns no diagnostics; an independently created governance setting caused no Terraform drift.
Shared stateLocal-to-Blob migration, a second checkout, actual concurrent lock rejection/release and return to local state passed using Entra managed identity over a private Blob endpoint. Lineage and all 8 original resource IDs were preserved.
Current release acceptanceThe Detection-default release was freshly deployed from its exact GitHub commit. Default Detection, the transition to Prevention, six baseline HTTP checks, three complete 32-check feature suites, 17 Azure configuration checks, failover/recovery and a primary Private Link region change passed. Final plans had no changes.
Repeat onboardingA fresh GitHub checkout created the documented eight resources. Four public/private coexistence checks and four checks after disabling app public access passed. Both stacks then had no-change plans.
CleanupAll 114 managed test resources across three validation rounds were removed. All six temporary resource groups were confirmed absent. The reused group/app were verified intact before their later intentional fixture cleanup.

Default update: the latest release was live-tested starting in its default Detection mode, then explicitly switched to Prevention. Both behaviors and the expanded configuration passed real Azure traffic checks.

Limits: custom DNS and both certificate options were deferred and were not live-tested. Identity/RBAC checks do not prove Key Vault certificate retrieval. Exclusions at all three scopes were accepted and read back, but runtime tests do not cover every managed rule or configuration combination. The backup app was in the same application region, using a different Private Link region; this was not a regional application disaster-recovery exercise.

The customer must still test its own login, API behavior, health paths, WAF false positives and deployment access. Event Hub delivery belongs to the separate diagnostics application. Azure configuration can take time to propagate; Terraform success is followed by actual application checks. Full results and limitations are in docs/validation.md.

12 · CUSTOMER DECISIONS

Values to confirm before production

No customer brand, subscription, app or region is hard-coded in this guide. Resolve the relevant items below; optional production features do not block testing the basic generated-hostname deployment.

1Names and subscription

Which subscription, resource group and naming convention should be used?

2Origins and regions

Which existing apps, actual hostnames, health paths and supported Private Link locations are approved? Are there residency restrictions?

3Access and cutover

Who approves private connections and changes app public access? Is the app currently serving public users?

4WAF rollout

Who reviews WAF logs and false positives during the default Detection phase, and who confirms the switch to Prevention after tuning?

5Optional production features

Which customer domains, certificates, API rewrites, caching rules or availability/failover targets are required?

6Operational ownership

Who owns deployment/state backups, monitoring and recovery, and when will a second operator require shared state?

REFERENCE

Glossary

TermMeaning
TerraformThe tool that compares declared configuration with recorded infrastructure and applies a reviewed plan.
AzureRMThe Terraform provider used here to manage Azure resources; this repository locks version 5.10.0.
SubscriptionThe Azure subscription selected by subscription_id for this Front Door deployment.
Resource groupThe Azure container holding the resources in this deployment. Its metadata location does not select the global edge location.
Front DoorAzure’s global HTTP/HTTPS entry and routing service; this repository requires its Premium tier.
EndpointThe public Front Door hostname clients connect to. Azure generates the actual azurefd.net hostname.
OriginA configured destination for Front Door, such as an existing Web App hostname and resource ID.
Origin groupA pool of origins for one routing destination, with health probes and load-balancing settings.
RouteA mapping from an endpoint/domain and URL patterns to an origin group.
Private LinkThe private connection used by Front Door to reach the origin. The origin owner approves its connection request.
WAFWeb Application Firewall: evaluates web requests against managed and customer-defined rules.
PreventionWAF mode that enforces configured rule actions, including blocking decisions.
DetectionWAF mode that evaluates matches without enforcing blocking actions; exported logs need the external diagnostics setup.
DRSMicrosoft Default Rule Set. This repository defaults to version 2.1; its anomaly scoring contributes to blocking decisions.
Managed identityAn Azure identity attached to the profile for supported resource access, such as Key Vault certificates.
StateTerraform’s record linking configuration to deployed resource IDs; it is not an application database or log store.
BackendThe location Terraform uses for its state: initially local, optionally Azure Blob storage later.
DNSThe records that map a customer hostname to Front Door and establish domain ownership.
TLSThe encryption/certificate layer used by HTTPS.
Event HubThe log-delivery destination configured by the separate diagnostics application, outside this repository.
RBACRole-based access control: permissions granted to an operator or identity at a defined Azure scope.
DriftA difference between the declared/recorded deployment and its current configuration in Azure.
